pharm: Synthetic progestin that produces secretory endometrial change, suppresses gonadotrophins, and prevents ovulation (depot form), used contraceptively and for menstrual/endometrial disorders.
quick: DMPA 150 mg IM every 3 months; oral 5-10 mg/day for menstrual disorders
Oral tablets may be taken with or without food
No specific adjustment; use with caution
Bone density (long-term depot), BP, weight, mood, bleeding pattern
summary: Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) is a synthetic progestin. The depot injectable suspension (DMPA, 150 mg IM) is a long-acting contraceptive given every three months that suppresses ovulation. Oral MPA (e.g. Provera) is used for secondary amenorrhoea, abnormal uterine bleeding due to hormonal imbalance, and to reduce endometrial hyperplasia when used with estrogen. The injectable form carries a boxed warning that prolonged use may cause significant, possibly not fully reversible, loss of bone mineral density.
indications: Abnormal uterine bleeding due to hormonal imbalance without organic pathology (oral)
Reduction of endometrial hyperplasia in postmenopausal women receiving estrogen (oral, adjunct)
Management of endometriosis-associated pain (depot subcutaneous, per labeling)

dosage.d: 150 mg of depot suspension every 3 months (every 12-13 weeks)
dosage.n: First dose within first 5 days of menses or per protocol; re-injection no later than 13 weeks
Begin at any time if pregnancy excluded

dosage.d: 5-10 mg daily for 5-10 days, starting on a calculated cycle day
dosage.n: Per cycle-day instructions; bleeding usually follows withdrawal

dosage.d: Typically 5-10 mg daily for 12-14 days per cycle or continuous low dose

admin: Shake the depot suspension vigorously before drawing up; inject deep IM (gluteal/deltoid) or SC per formulation
Schedule re-injection so it is not delayed beyond the recommended interval; exclude pregnancy if late
Take oral tablets at the same time each day for the prescribed number of days
Counsel on irregular bleeding/spotting, which is common early on
For long-term depot use, ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D intake and weight-bearing exercise
moa: Medroxyprogesterone acetate binds progesterone receptors and exerts progestational effects. In contraceptive depot use it suppresses hypothalamic-pituitary release of gonadotrophins (LH surge), thereby inhibiting ovulation; it also thickens cervical mucus and renders the endometrium unfavourable for implantation. In menstrual and endometrial uses, it transforms proliferative endometrium into secretory endometrium and, on withdrawal, produces a controlled bleed, while opposing estrogen-driven endometrial hyperplasia.

absolute: Known or suspected breast cancer or other progestin-sensitive malignancy
Active thromboembolic disorder (or history of thrombophlebitis, DVT, pulmonary embolism, cerebrovascular disease)
relative: Risk factors for osteoporosis (for long-term depot)
Fluid-retention conditions (asthma, migraine, epilepsy, cardiac/renal dysfunction)
monitor: Bone mineral density with prolonged depot use

preg: Contraindicated in known or suspected pregnancy. Progestins are not indicated to maintain pregnancy. If exposure occurs in early pregnancy, counsel the patient; available data do not show a clear major teratogenic effect, but use is not appropriate during pregnancy.
lact: Progestin-only medroxyprogesterone is considered compatible with breastfeeding and does not adversely affect milk quantity or quality; small amounts pass into milk. Depot contraception is widely used in lactating women.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is established; use with caution in patients with conditions worsened by fluid retention.
hepatic: Contraindicated in significant or active hepatic disease. Discontinue if jaundice or signs of liver dysfunction develop, as steroids are hepatically metabolised.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort - may reduce efficacy of oral progestin)
moderate: CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole - may raise levels)
interactions.food: Oral tablets may be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; moderate alcohol use is acceptable.
interactions.diagnostics: May alter results of liver, thyroid, coagulation, and endocrine (e.g. metyrapone) function tests; can affect glucose tolerance test results.

serious: Loss of bone mineral density (depot, prolonged use)
rare: Worsening of migraine with focal symptoms
emergency: Signs of thrombosis (sudden leg pain/swelling, chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, visual loss)

monitoring: Bone mineral density if depot used beyond 2 years
Glucose in diabetics; liver function if symptomatic
counsel: Irregular bleeding or no periods is common early on and usually settles; periods may take time to return after stopping the depot
For long-term injections, take enough calcium and vitamin D and do weight-bearing exercise to protect bones
Return on time for your 3-monthly injection so contraception is not interrupted
Seek urgent care for leg swelling/pain, chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, or vision changes
Tell your doctor about low mood, and about epilepsy, migraine, diabetes, or liver problems
pk: Oral progestational effect within days; depot ovulation suppression within ~24 h
Oral peak ~2-4 h; depot plateau over weeks
Oral ~12-17 h; depot persists for months (apparent ~50 days)
Depot contraceptive effect about 3 months per dose
Store at 20-25 C; do not freeze the injectable suspension; protect from light
pearls: Boxed warning (depot): prolonged use causes significant, possibly not fully reversible, loss of bone mineral density - not recommended beyond 2 years unless other methods are inadequate
Return of fertility after the depot can be delayed (median ~10 months from last injection)
Irregular bleeding then amenorrhoea is the expected bleeding pattern - counsel up front to improve adherence
Oral MPA opposes estrogen-driven endometrial hyperplasia in hormone therapy
missed: For oral therapy, take a missed dose as soon as remembered unless the next dose is near, then skip it. For the depot injection, if you are late (beyond 13 weeks for IM), use back-up contraception and have pregnancy excluded before re-injection.
overdose: Overdose of progestin is generally not associated with serious acute toxicity; symptoms may include nausea, drowsiness, and withdrawal bleeding. There is no specific antidote; treatment is supportive. The long-acting depot cannot be removed once injected, so effects persist.
